C005.subject: acute sleep deprivation
C005.object: spatial working memory only when task requires dynamic updating
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: acute sleep deprivation spatial working memory only when task requires dynamic updating]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled laboratory experiment comparing performance on spatial working memory tasks with and without dynamic updating (e.g., n-back vs. static location recall) under 24-hour sleep deprivation vs. rested control — Directly tests the hypothesis by isolating the dynamic updating requirement as a moderating factor, enabling causal inference through within-subject or between-group design.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on sleep deprivation and working memory, focusing on task type (dynamic updating vs. maintenance-only) as a moderator — Synthesizes available evidence to assess whether the effect is consistently observed across studies, addressing the disputed status and providing statistical power to confirm or refute the moderation claim.

[PATH:empirical] Neuroimaging study (fMRI or EEG) comparing brain activation patterns (e.g., prefrontal cortex, hippocampus) during spatial working memory tasks with and without dynamic updating under acute sleep loss — Provides mechanistic evidence: if dynamic updating tasks uniquely recruit regions vulnerable to sleep deprivation (e.g., dorsolateral prefrontal cortex), this supports the hypothesis; absence of differential activation would refute it.

scope.domain: cognitive performance under 24-hour sleep loss with task type moderation

qualifier.temporal: within 24 hours of sleep loss onset

C006.subject: acute sleep deprivation
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: acute sleep deprivation spatial working memory]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled laboratory study comparing performance on the N-back task (spatial variant) under 24-hour total sleep deprivation vs. rested wakefulness, with counterbalanced within-subject design and actigraphy monitoring. — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring spatial working memory accuracy and reaction time after acute sleep loss, controlling for circadian confounds and practice effects.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies (fMRI, PET) examining prefrontal and parietal activation patterns during spatial working memory tasks under sleep deprivation. — Synthesizes existing evidence to determine whether neural correlates of spatial working memory are preserved or altered, providing a higher-level assessment of the disputed claim.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis based on the resource depletion model vs. the compensatory recruitment hypothesis, predicting differential effects on spatial vs. verbal working memory under sleep loss. — Helps clarify the mechanism underlying the hypothesis and identifies boundary conditions (e.g., task difficulty, individual differences) that could explain conflicting findings.

C007.subject: chronic partial sleep deprivation
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: chronic partial sleep deprivation verbal working memory]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled laboratory study comparing verbal n-back task performance in participants undergoing 5+ days of 5-6 hours sleep vs. 8 hours sleep, with simultaneous fMRI monitoring of prefrontal cortex activation — Directly tests the cumulative effect of partial sleep deprivation on verbal working memory under high cognitive load, and can measure whether prefrontal metabolic decline (e.g., reduced BOLD signal) occurs despite compensatory neural recruitment in other regions.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on partial sleep restriction (≥5 days) and working memory outcomes, focusing on verbal vs. spatial tasks and moderating effects of task difficulty — Synthesizes existing evidence to determine if the effect is consistently found across studies, and whether the proposed mechanism (prefrontal decline vs. compensation) is supported by neuroimaging data from multiple labs.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational model of prefrontal cortex metabolic dynamics during repeated sleep restriction, simulating cumulative decline in glucose metabolism and its impact on verbal working memory capacity — Tests the mechanistic plausibility of cumulative prefrontal metabolic decline as a cause of impairment, and can generate predictions about threshold effects or individual differences in compensatory recruitment.

scope.domain: repeated mild sleep restriction over 5+ days with high cognitive load demands

qualifier.mechanism: cumulative prefrontal cortex metabolic decline overriding compensatory neural recruitment

C008.subject: chronic partial sleep deprivation
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: chronic partial sleep deprivation verbal working memory]

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of polysomnography-controlled sleep restriction studies measuring verbal working memory via n-back or digit span tasks (2000–2020) — A meta-analysis of existing laboratory studies can clarify the disputed effect by pooling small-sample findings, controlling for confounds like total sleep time vs. sleep fragmentation, and assessing publication bias.

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing 5 nights of 5-hour sleep opportunity vs. 8-hour sleep in healthy adults, with pre/post fMRI during a verbal n-back task — Direct empirical test under controlled conditions using neuroimaging can isolate the specific impairment in verbal working memory from general fatigue or attentional lapses, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:empirical] Re-analysis of individual participant data from the Wisconsin Sleep Cohort or similar longitudinal datasets, focusing on self-reported sleep restriction and objective verbal memory outcomes — Leveraging existing large-scale data with repeated measures can provide ecological validity and statistical power to confirm or refute the effect in real-world settings, complementing lab studies.

scope.domain: repeated mild sleep restriction over 5+ days

qualifier.geographic: primarily laboratory settings in North America and Europe

C011.subject: total sleep deprivation
C011.object: emotional working memory for positive stimuli
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: total sleep deprivation emotional working memory for positive stimuli]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled laboratory study using an emotional n-back task with positively valenced images (e.g., from the International Affective Picture System) after 36 hours of total sleep deprivation vs. rested controls — Directly tests the hypothesis under the specified scope (36 hours awake) with a standard measure of emotional working memory, allowing comparison of accuracy and reaction times for positive stimuli.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of existing literature on sleep deprivation and emotional working memory, focusing on valence-specific effects — Synthesizes available evidence to determine whether the impairment for positive stimuli is consistently observed across studies, addressing the disputed status and clarifying effect size and direction.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational model of affective-cognitive interaction under sleep loss, incorporating dopamine and prefrontal cortex resource depletion — Provides mechanistic predictions about why positive stimuli might be differentially affected (e.g., reward sensitivity changes), offering a falsifiable framework to guide further empirical tests.

C012.subject: total sleep deprivation
C012.object: emotional working memory for negative stimuli
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: total sleep deprivation emotional working memory for negative stimuli]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled laboratory experiment comparing emotional working memory performance (e.g., n-back task with negative, neutral, and positive images) between a total sleep deprivation group (36 hours awake) and a rested control group, with pre- and post-deprivation measures. — Directly tests the causal effect of 36-hour wakefulness on emotional working memory for negative stimuli, controlling for confounds like circadian phase and task practice effects.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on sleep deprivation and emotional memory, focusing on studies that include working memory tasks with emotional valence. — Aggregates existing evidence to determine whether the effect is consistent across methodologies, sample sizes, and stimulus types, and to assess potential publication bias.

[PATH:empirical] Neuroimaging study (fMRI or EEG) examining changes in prefrontal-amygdala connectivity during an emotional working memory task after 36 hours of wakefulness. — Provides mechanistic evidence: if sleep deprivation disrupts top-down regulation of amygdala by prefrontal cortex specifically for negative stimuli, that would support the hypothesis; if connectivity changes are not valence-specific, it would refute the claim of selective impairment.
